<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

</span>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Universal Speech Enhancement (USE) aims to restore speech quality under diverse degradation conditions while preserving signal fidelity. Despite recent progress, key challenges in training target selection, the distortion–perception tradeoff, and data curation remain unresolved. In this work, we systematically address these three overlooked problems. First, we revisit the conventional practice of using early-reflected speech as the dereverberation target and show that it can degrade perceptual quality and downstream ASR performance. We instead demonstrate that time-shifted anechoic clean speech provides a superior learning target. Second, guided by the distortion–perception tradeoff theory, we propose a simple two-stage framework that achieves minimal distortion under a given level of perceptual quality. Third, we analyze the trade-off between training data scale and quality for USE, revealing that training on large uncurated corpora imposes a performance ceiling, as models struggle to remove subtle artifacts. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the URGENT 2025 non-blind test set and exhibits strong language-agnostic generalization, making it effective for improving TTS training data. Model weights are available for download at: <a href="https://huggingface.co/nvidia/RE-USE" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://huggingface.co/nvidia/RE-USE</a>.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Universal speech enhancement (USE)<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Serrà et al. (2022)</a></cite> aims to improve the intelligibility and perceptual quality of degraded speech across diverse conditions while preserving attributes such as speaker identity, emotion and accent <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Babaev et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
Recent research has increasingly shifted from task-specific methods toward generalized models capable of handling heterogeneous domains and conditions.
For instance, VoiceFixer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2021</a>)</cite> combines a ResUNet-based analysis stage with a neural vocoder-based synthesis stage, while MaskSR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024</a>)</cite> employs a masked generative modeling objective to handle comparable conditions. More recently, AnyEnhance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025a</a>)</cite> introduced prompt-guidance and a self-critic mechanism, offering a unified framework capable of mitigating diverse degradations across speech and singing voice.
To further advance this generalization, the URGENT 2025 Challenge <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Saijo et al., 2025</a>)</cite> established a standardized training data from diverse sources with varying quality covering seven distortion types (additive noise, reverberation, clipping, bandwidth limitation, codec artifacts, packet loss, and wind noise) across multiple sampling rates (8, 16, 22.05, 24, 32, 44.1, and 48 kHz) and five languages (English, German, French, Spanish, and Chinese). Adopting this rigorous setup, we investigate three previously overlooked bottlenecks: (1) training target selection, (2) the trade-off between fidelity and perceptual quality, and (3) training data curation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold">Training Targets</span>: In the URGENT Challenge, six of the seven speech distortions use original anechoic clean speech as the training target. However, for <span id="S1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">dereverberation</span>, the standard target is <span id="S1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">early-reflected speech</span>, derived by convolving original anechoic clean speech with the early reflection component of the room impulse response (RIR).
This convention stems from the common belief that ”removing early reflections is challenging and may introduce excessive artifacts”  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Valin et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2020</a>)</cite>.
Contrary to this view, we found that retaining early reflections for training degrades both perceptual quality and machine intelligibility measured by downstream ASR performance.
We argue that the primary difficulty in dereverberation is not the early reflections themselves, but the misalignment between the reverberant input and clean target caused by the implicit estimation of the <span id="S1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">direct-path time shift</span>.
We propose using time-shifted anechoic clean speech as the learning target, which resolved this misalignment and significantly boosts performance.
While previous studies have used similar targets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, we provide the first systematic, large-scale evaluation of these two targets under diverse degradation conditions and demonstrate the superiority of the time-shifted anechoic clean target.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold">Model Architecture</span>: Existing approaches often struggle to balance signal fidelity and perceptual quality. For example, in the URGENT Challenge, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2025</a>)</cite> proposes a regression model that introduces a channel-mixing module to bridge time- and frequency-domain modeling, together with progressive block extension to enable model training at different scales. Although effective overall, its quality is inherently limited, as it tends to produce over-smoothed outputs under severe bandwidth limitations and packet loss  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Saijo et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
In contrast, purely generative approaches may improve perceptual quality but risk introducing hallucinated contents  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Saijo et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
In this Challenge, hybrid methods therefore explore ways to integrate the outputs of regression and generative models.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chao et al., 2025</a>)</cite> combines the two outputs using a simple energy-based criterion computed from the noisy input. Both <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rong et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Goswami and Harada, 2025</a>)</cite> propose three-stage frameworks to generate the final USE output: <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rong et al., 2025</a>)</cite> uses filling, separation, and restoration modules, while <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Goswami and Harada, 2025</a>)</cite> uses a fusion network that combines regression outputs with a token sampling-based generative model. Going further, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Le et al., 2025</a>)</cite> applies a four-stage strategy composed of audio declipping, packet loss compensation, audio separation, and spectral inpainting. <span id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">An important question, therefore, is which combination strategy is optimal and theoretically justified</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Motivated by the theoretical distortion-perception tradeoff (see Section <a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2 Bridging Fidelity and Quality: A Two-Stage Framework ‣ 2 Proposed Method ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a> and <a href="#A1.SS1" title="A.1 The Distortion-Perception Tradeoff ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.1</span></a> in the Appendix), we propose a streamlined two-stage framework that effectively combines the strengths of both paradigms. We first train a regression model to convergence (ensuring high fidelity) and freeze it. Its output then serves as a conditional input to a generative model (restoring perceptual details). This approach eliminates the complex heuristics of prior multi-stage methods while achieving optimal signal fidelity under a perceptual-quality constraint, with theoretical support provided in Section <a href="#A1.SS1" title="A.1 The Distortion-Perception Tradeoff ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.1</span></a> of the Appendix.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold">Training Data Quality</span>:
Deep learning models are fundamentally constrained by their data. While scaling laws regarding data quantity are well-studied <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gonzalez et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, the impact of data <span id="S1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">quality</span> in large-scale USE remains underexplored, with only one concurrent work hinting at its importance  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. We analyze the URGENT Challenge data and find that despite organizer filtering, many “clean” samples contain significant residual degradations, not only due to the use of early-reflected speech (Section <a href="#S2.SS3" title="2.3 Trade-off Between Training Data Scale and Quality ‣ 2 Proposed Method ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.3</span></a>). We demonstrate that training on such imperfect data imposes a hard performance ceiling, preventing models from removing subtle artifacts like electrical microphone hiss. We provide a detailed example of how data curation directly impacts performance to unseen real-world conditions (Section <a href="#S3.SS9" title="3.9 Evaluation on Unseen Languages ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.9</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">In summary, our work makes the following contributions:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">1. We critically reassess dereverberation learning targets, showing that time-shifted anechoic clean speech consistently outperforms early-reflection targets in USE settings.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">2. We propose a theoretically grounded two-stage framework that achieves an optimal fidelity–perception trade-off.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">3. We conduct a comprehensive analysis of the trade-off between training data quality and quantity, highlighting the importance of data curation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Proposed Method</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we analyze key challenges in universal speech enhancement and present our proposed solutions.
First, we address the limitations of conventional dereverberation targets and justify using time-shifted anechoic clean speech.
Second, we introduce a two-stage framework that effectively combines regression and generative models to resovle the fidelity-quality dilemma.
Finally, we investigate the critical trade-off between training data scale and quality, a relatively new topic that has been seldom explored.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Shifted Anechoic Clean Speech as a Superior Learning Target</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.3" class="ltx_p">Given an anechoic clean speech <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> and an RIR <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>, the reverberant speech <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> is modeled as the convolution between them:</p>

<p id="S2.SS1.p1.4" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the discrete time index, <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ast" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∗</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ast</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the convolution operator. The RIR <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r[n]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r[n]</annotation></semantics></math> can be decomposed into the direct path <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta[n-n_{0}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta[n-n_{0}]</annotation></semantics></math>, early reflection <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{e}[n]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{e}[n]</annotation></semantics></math>, and late reflection <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{l}[n]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{l}[n]</annotation></semantics></math> (see Figure <a href="#A1.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ A.3 Limitations ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> in Appendix):</p>

<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.5" class="ltx_p">Here, <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta[n]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta[n]</annotation></semantics></math> is the Dirac delta function, and <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> represents the direct-path time shift (typically 5–30 ms). We estimate <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> based on the maximum magnitude of the RIR, i.e., <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{0}=\arg\max_{n}|r[n]|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>max</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{0}=\arg\max_{n}|r[n]|</annotation></semantics></math>. Early reflections are defined as RIR components occurring within 50 ms after the direct-path peak <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta[n-n_{0}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta[n-n_{0}]</annotation></semantics></math> as specified in the URGENT Challenge
 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Saijo et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024b</a>)</cite> and other studies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, while subsequent impulses components constitute late reflections <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Naylor and Gaubitch, 2010</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Conventional dereverberation approaches, including the URGENT Challenge, typically use early-reflected speech <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{e}[n]=s[n]\ast\delta[n-n_{0}]\ast r_{e}[n]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{e}[n]=s[n]\ast\delta[n-n_{0}]\ast r_{e}[n]</annotation></semantics></math> as the learning target. This convention stems from the belief that <span id="S2.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">“early reflections are much harder to remove, and the difficulty of solving the problem leads to excessive artifacts in the enhanced speech”</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Valin et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2020</a>)</cite>. Indeed, we found that using the unshifted anechoic clean signal <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s[n]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s[n]</annotation></semantics></math> directly as a target yields the poorest performance (Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.4 Results on Training Data Filtering Based on Quality Estimation ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a><span id="S2.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text">(b)</span>), aligning with prior findings.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Although early reflections have a smaller impact on perceived quality compared to late reverberation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Valin et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, we find that retaining early reflections still significantly degrades speech quality metrics (UTMOS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Saeki et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, DNSMOS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Reddy et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, NISQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mittag et al., 2021</a>)</cite>).
As shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.4 Results on Training Data Filtering Based on Quality Estimation ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a><span id="S2.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text">(b)</span>, progressively reducing the early reflection window from 50 ms to 0 ms consistently improves quality scores of the enhanced speech.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Setting the window to 0 ms reduces the target to the time-shifted anechoic signal of <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>, as <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s[n]\ast\delta[n-n_{0}]=s[n-n_{0}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s[n]\ast\delta[n-n_{0}]=s[n-n_{0}]</annotation></semantics></math>. Consequently, in Equation (<a href="#S2.E2" title="In 2.1 Shifted Anechoic Clean Speech as a Superior Learning Target ‣ 2 Proposed Method ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>), eliminating early reflections poses little difficulty for the model. The critical challenge is the implicit estimation of the <span id="S2.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">direct-path time shift</span>, which introduces a misalignment of <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> between the reverberant input and the clean target.
By using the time-shifted target <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s[n-n_{0}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s[n-n_{0}]</annotation></semantics></math>, we effectively bypass this alignment issue. This confirms that <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s[n-n_{0}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s[n-n_{0}]</annotation></semantics></math> outperforms the conventional early-reflected target (<math id="S2.SS1.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{e}[n]=s[n]\ast\delta[n-n_{0}]\ast r_{e}[n]=s[n-n_{0}]\ast r_{e}[n]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{e}[n]=s[n]\ast\delta[n-n_{0}]\ast r_{e}[n]=s[n-n_{0}]\ast r_{e}[n]</annotation></semantics></math>), and outperforms further the original clean speech <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s[n]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s[n]</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Bridging Fidelity and Quality: A Two-Stage Framework</h3>

<figure id="S2.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2603.02641v4/figs/Picture1.png" id="S2.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:333/117;" width="333" height="117" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S2.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Motivated by the distortion–perception tradeoff theory, the proposed two-stage framework integrates a frozen regression model with a residual generative model.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">According to the distortion–perception tradeoff theory <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Blau and Michaeli, 2018</a>)</cite> shown in computer vision applications, speech restoration also faces a fundamental trade-off between <span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">fidelity</span> (preserving linguistic content, speaker identity, emotion, and accent) and <span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">perceptual quality</span>.
Generative and regression (also called discriminative) models tackle the problem in distinct ways. The regression model outputs the conditional expectation, <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{s}=E[S\mid Y=y]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{s}=E[S\mid Y=y]</annotation></semantics></math>, whereas the generative model produces samples from the conditional distribution, <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{s}\sim p(s\mid y)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{s}\sim p(s\mid y)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to the degraded input speech signal.
Under severe degradation like packet loss, bandwidth limitation, and low SNR, <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> contains little information about the true clean signal so that
the regression output is biased towards prior mean <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E[S\mid Y=y]\approx E[S]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E[S\mid Y=y]\approx E[S]</annotation></semantics></math>. If the prior is multimodal (e.g., many plausible phonemes), the mean may be a blend of modes, which sounds muffled and unnatural, resulting in <span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">over-smoothing problem</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ren et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chao et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Conversely, in such a scenario, the generative model produces outputs drawn from the prior distribution, <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(s\mid y)\approx p(s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(s\mid y)\approx p(s)</annotation></semantics></math>, enabling the generation of natural-sounding speech consistent with the prior. Nevertheless, the lexical/linguistic content or speaker characteristics are not guaranteed to match the original signal, resulting in <span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">hallucination problem</span> as defined in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Saijo et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Scheibler et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. In summary, when <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> is less informative, the regression model excels at preserving fidelity but may fail to improve quality, whereas the generative model enhances quality but often struggles to preserve fidelity.
Specifically, posterior sampling from the posterior <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(s\mid y)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(s\mid y)</annotation></semantics></math> results in a mean squared error (MSE) that is twice the minimum MSE (MMSE), which is achieved by the regression model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Blau and Michaeli, 2018</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We address this trade-off by leveraging insights from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Freirich et al. (2021)</a></cite>, which suggest that an optimal distortion-perception balance—minimizing MSE while satisfying the constraint of perfect perception—can be achieved by <span id="S2.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">optimally transporting</span> the posterior mean (MMSE estimate) toward the true data distribution (the derivation is provided in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS1" title="A.1 The Distortion-Perception Tradeoff ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.1</span></a>).
We further argue that <span id="S2.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">preserving fidelity, particularly linguistic content, is usually paramount</span> in applications of universal speech enhancement.
Therefore, we propose a sequential strategy that first uses a regression model to estimate the posterior mean, and then applies a generative model to correct only the over-smoothed regions through optimal transport (see Figure <a href="#S2.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 2.2 Bridging Fidelity and Quality: A Two-Stage Framework ‣ 2 Proposed Method ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>):</p>
<ol id="S2.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Regression Stage:</span> We first train a regression model to convergence to estimate the posterior mean (<math id="S2.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{s}=E[S\mid Y=y]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{s}=E[S\mid Y=y]</annotation></semantics></math>), maximizing fidelity. We then freeze its weights.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Generative Stage:</span> We then employ a generative model to optimally transport the posterior mean toward the true data distribution by minimizing the Wasserstein distance (<math id="S2.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{2}(p_{\hat{s}},p_{s})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{2}(p_{\hat{s}},p_{s})</annotation></semantics></math>).
Crucially, we employ a residual connection between the regression model output and the final output, forcing the generative model to focus primarily on regions where characteristics diverge from those of real data to restore perceptual details.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Previous work approximates the optimal transport using flow matching and achieves improved MSE in image restoration <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ohayon et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. In addition to speech enhancement  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Serbest et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, SEStream <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and StoRM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lemercier et al., 2023</a>)</cite> also achieve strong results in codec compression and dereverberation, respectively, by using a regression model to provide an initial prediction for a subsequent generative model. In this study, we leverage GAN-based methods to approximate optimal transport. Wasserstein GANs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arjovsky et al., 2017</a>)</cite> optimize an objective equivalent to the Wasserstein-1 distance between the source and target distributions, a principled metric from optimal transport theory. Furthermore, as future work toward adapting the model to real-time scenarios, the single forward-pass generation of GAN offers lower computational latency.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p4.2" class="ltx_p">Beyond the formal derivation in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS1" title="A.1 The Distortion-Perception Tradeoff ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.1</span></a>, we offer an alternative explanation of why GANs can <span id="S2.SS2.p4.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">focus on correcting over-smoothed regions while leaving other parts unchanged</span>. When a convolutional neural network (CNN) is employed as the discriminator, each element of the final feature map (the layer before the averaging operation used to produce the final prediction) has only a limited receptive field. Assuming the discriminator is Lipschitz continuous (e.g., via spectral normalization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Miyato et al., 2018</a>)</cite>), the following constraint holds:</p>
<table id="S2.E3" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S2.E3X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E3X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\|D^{(l)}(\tilde{s})-D^{(l)}(s)\|\leq L\|\tilde{s}-s\|,\quad\forall l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msup><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>−</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\|D^{(l)}(\tilde{s})-D^{(l)}(s)\|\leq L\|\tilde{s}-s\|,\quad\forall l</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="D^{(l)}(.)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D^{(l)}(.)</annotation></semantics></math> is the <math id="S2.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math>-th discriminator layer, <math id="S2.SS2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> is the Lipschitz constant, and <math id="S2.SS2.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{s}</annotation></semantics></math> is the final model output. Here, let us focus on the receptive field of one element in the final feature map. The distance between the receptive field <math id="S2.SS2.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{s}</annotation></semantics></math> and the corresponding clean speech <math id="S2.SS2.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> serves as an <span id="S2.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">upper bound</span> on the left-hand side of Equation (<a href="#S2.E3" title="In 2.2 Bridging Fidelity and Quality: A Two-Stage Framework ‣ 2 Proposed Method ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>), which corresponds to the <span id="S2.SS2.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">feature-matching loss</span> used during generator training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Salimans et al. (2016)</a></cite>.
When the model accurately predicts the clean target within the receptive field (i.e., <math id="S2.SS2.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lVert\tilde{s}-s\rVert\approx 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>−</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0.1389em">∥</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.1389em">≈</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lVert\tilde{s}-s\rVert\approx 0</annotation></semantics></math>), Equation (<a href="#S2.E3" title="In 2.2 Bridging Fidelity and Quality: A Two-Stage Framework ‣ 2 Proposed Method ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>) ensures that the feature-matching loss does not contribute gradients for these regions. Therefore, the generative model can mainly focus on correcting the over-smoothed regions of the regression model output (see Figures <a href="#A1.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ A.3 Limitations ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> and <a href="#A1.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ A.3 Limitations ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> in the Appendix for spectrogram visualization). Consequently, this two-stage framework can keep the fidelity while improving speech quality.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Trade-off Between Training Data Scale and Quality</h3>

<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2603.02641v4/figs/All_median.png" id="S2.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:248/186;" width="248" height="186" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S2.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Histogram of VQScore for URGENT 2025 Challenge Track 1 subsets. Dashed lines indicate median scores.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The URGENT 2025 Challenge (Track 1) provides approximately 2,500 hours of speech from diverse sources, including CommonVoice <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ardila et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, DNS5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dubey et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, MLS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pratap et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, LibriTTS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zen et al., 2019</a>)</cite>, VCTK <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Veaux et al., 2013</a>)</cite>, WSJ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Garofolo et al., 1993</a>)</cite>, and EARS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Richter et al., 2024</a>)</cite> as summarized in Table <a href="#A1.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ A.3 Limitations ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> (Appendix). Although the organizers have already filtered out non-speech samples using voice activity detection (VAD) and removed noisy samples based on the DNSMOS score, many recordings with audible background noise remain there <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Saijo et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Leveraging its high correlation with subjective scores <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025b</a>)</cite> and fast inference capability (processing 2,500 hours of speech in less than 8 hours on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU), we employ VQScore <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fu et al., 2024</a>)</cite> to analyze the quality distribution of each training data source. Figure <a href="#S2.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 2.3 Trade-off Between Training Data Scale and Quality ‣ 2 Proposed Method ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> illustrates the VQScore distribution for each speech source (individual source histograms are provided in Figure <a href="#A1.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ A.3 Limitations ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> in the Appendix).</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We observe a clear quality hierarchy: CommonVoice, the largest subset (1,300 hours), exhibits the lowest quality due to its crowdsourced nature.
Conversely, datasets like WSJ, EARS, and VCTK show consistently top-3 highest quality.
Manual inspection reveals that low-VQScore samples often contain stationary background noise or entirely non-speech artifacts (examples are provided in the supplementary material).
These training targets can confuse the speech enhancement model and degrade its performance.
To mitigate this, we apply a VQScore threshold to <span id="S2.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">further</span> filter low-quality samples. Finally, we leverage the high quality of the EARS dataset for a final fine-tuning stage. (Section <a href="#S3.SS9" title="3.9 Evaluation on Unseen Languages ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.9</span></a>). Note that some extremely expressive EARS samples (e.g., whispering) receive low VQScore ratings, however, the dataset remains the cleanest overall source available.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Experiments</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Dataset</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As noted earlier, the URGENT 2025 Challenge training dataset comprises multi-condition speech recordings across five languages (English, German, French, Spanish, and Chinese) with diverse sampling frequencies (8, 16, 22.05, 24, 32, 44.1, and 48 kHz), along with noise samples and RIRs. Seven types of distortions are considered: additive noise, reverberation, clipping, bandwidth limitation, codec artifacts, packet loss, and wind noise. We followed the organizers’ guidelines to simulate the validation set using the validation splits of the corpora <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Saijo et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. The non-blind test set of URGENT 2025, consisting of 1,000 utterances, is used for evaluation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Model Architecture</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To enable a single model to operate across different sampling rates, we employ sampling frequency-independent (SFI) STFT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2023a</a>)</cite>, which dynamically adjusts the FFT window and hop size according to the input sampling rate, ensuring a fixed time duration and consistent feature frame length across all sampling rates. To ensure that inputs with different sampling rates yield an integer number of frequency bins, we set the FFT window size to 320 points for the 8 kHz case
(corresponding to a 40 ms window for all sampling rates).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Since the model architecture is not the primary focus of this paper, we adopt USEMamba with 30 layers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chao et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chao et al., 2024</a>)</cite> as the regression model. USEMamba alternates between two types of sequence modeling modules (i.e., Mamba) applied to frequency features and time features in the time-frequency domain. For GAN training, we use a 6-layer USEMamba as the generator and CNN-based discriminators.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To account for distinct feature patterns across frequency bands and support speech with varying sampling rates, we propose an <span id="S3.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">adaptive multi-band discriminator</span>, inspired by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kumar et al. (2023)</a></cite>. For each band corresponding to the input sampling rate (e.g., for 8 kHz, a single sub-band from 0-4 kHz; for 22.05 kHz, three sub-bands: 0-4 kHz, 4-8 kHz, and 8-11.025 kHz), we use a 5-layer 2-D convolutional network for local feature extraction. Sub-band features are concatenated along the frequency axis and passed through a final 2-layer 2-D convolution followed by global average pooling to produce the discriminator output. All models are trained on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs with a batch size of 1, allowing longer utterances to be processed without memory issues. We use AdamW with a learning rate of 0.0002 for the regression model, generator, and discriminator. The code will be released upon acceptance to facilitate reproducibility.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Evaluation Metrics</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To address the dual objectives of improving perceptual quality and maintaining signal fidelity, we employ a comprehensive suite of metrics.
For standard reference-based evaluation, we report Perceptual Evaluation of Speech Quality (PESQ) for perceptual quality <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rix et al., 2001</a>)</cite>, Extended Short-Time Objective Intelligibility (ESTOI) for intelligibility <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jensen and Taal, 2016</a>)</cite>, and Signal-to-Distortion Ratio (SDR) for time-domain waveform distortion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Roux et al., 2019</a>)</cite>. Spectral deviation is further assessed using Mel Cepstral Distortion (MCD) and Log-Spectral Distance (LSD).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We also evaluate performance on downstream tasks using both task-independent and task-dependent measures. Task-independent metrics include SpeechBERTScore (SBERT) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Saeki et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, which utilizes self-supervised models to quantify enhancement quality, and Levenshtein Phoneme Similarity (LPS) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pirklbauer et al., 2023</a>)</cite> for phoneme sequence similarity. Task-dependent metrics include speaker similarity (SpkSim) to measure speaker identity preservation and character accuracy (CAcc) to reflect ASR performance  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">Peng et al. (2024)</a></cite>. Finally, we report non-intrusive metrics, including DNSMOS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Reddy et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, NISQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mittag et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, and UTMOS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Saeki et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, which estimate perceptual quality without requiring a clean reference.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Most Metrics (excluding non-intrusive ones and CAcc) require a clean speech reference. However, for the speech dereverberation task, the organizers provide <span id="S3.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">early-reflected speech</span> as the clean reference <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Saijo et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. This creates a definition mismatch, as our model is trained on time-shifted anechoic clean speech. <span id="S3.SS3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Consequently, this discrepancy may penalize our leaderboard scores on reference-based metrics such as PESQ, ESTOI, SDR, MCD, LSD, SBERT, LPS, and SpkSim</span>, underestimating performance compared to the actual perceptual quality and fidelity obtained when using the original anechoic speech as the reference, as reported in Table <a href="#A1.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ A.2 Ablation study ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> in the Appendix.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Results on Training Data Filtering Based on Quality Estimation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Based on the observations in Section <a href="#S2.SS3" title="2.3 Trade-off Between Training Data Scale and Quality ‣ 2 Proposed Method ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.3</span></a>, we first determine an appropriate VQScore threshold, such that training samples with scores below the threshold are excluded. We consider three thresholds: 0.50 (no filtering), 0.65, and 0.72, corresponding to 2,518 (original size), 2,506, and 629 hours of training data, respectively. We then train three models on these datasets using time-shifted anechoic clean speech as targets and plot the UTMOS learning curves on the validation set in Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.4 Results on Training Data Filtering Based on Quality Estimation ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a><span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">(a)</span>. Without VQScore filtering (<span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#0FE3FF;">blue line</span>), the model performs the worst, <span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">even though the Challenge organizers already removed speech samples with DNSMOS scores below 3</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Saijo et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. With a threshold of 0.72 (<span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#80FF00;">green line</span>), the model initially achieves the best performance in the early stage of training due to the higher data quality, but later lags behind the model trained with a threshold of 0.65 (<span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF7D00;">orange line</span>), likely due to the reduced data volumn. Based on these results,
we adopt a threshold of 0.65 in subsequent experiments, as it provides a good balance between training data quality and quantity.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S3.F3.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2603.02641v4/figs/UTMos_VqScore_grid.png" id="S3.F3.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:229/174;" width="229" height="174" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F3.sf1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(a)</span> </span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S3.F3.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2603.02641v4/figs/UTMos_Targets.png" id="S3.F3.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:229/174;" width="229" height="174" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F3.sf2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(b)</span> </span></figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S3.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Learning curves of UTMOS scores on the validation set under (a) different VQScore filtering thresholds and (b) different learning targets.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.5 </span>Results of Applying Time-Shifted Anechoic Clean Speech as Learning Targets</h3>

<div id="S3.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first examine the UTMOS learning curves under different training targets, shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.4 Results on Training Data Filtering Based on Quality Estimation ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a><span id="S3.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">(b)</span>. As discussed in Section <a href="#S2.SS1" title="2.1 Shifted Anechoic Clean Speech as a Superior Learning Target ‣ 2 Proposed Method ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>, directly using the original anechoic clean speech <math id="S3.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s[n]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s[n]</annotation></semantics></math> (<span id="S3.SS5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#0FE3FF;">blue line</span>) as the learning target yields the worst performance, consistent with previous studies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Valin et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2020</a>)</cite>. Therefore, we exclude this learning target from subsequent evaluations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3.5 Results of Applying Time-Shifted Anechoic Clean Speech as Learning Targets ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> reports the non-blind test results of our proposed approach, which uses time-shifted anechoic clean speech <math id="S3.SS5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s[n-n_{0}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s[n-n_{0}]</annotation></semantics></math> as the dereverberation target, alongside the baseline TF-GridNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and the top three ranked systems in the challenge
(Rank 1: Team Bobbsun <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, Rank 2: Team rc <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chao et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, Rank 3: Team Xiaobin <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rong et al., 2025</a>)</cite>).
The full leaderboard is publicly available <span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
              
              
              
            https://urgent-challenge.github.io/urgent2025/leaderboard/</span></span></span> and as presented in Table <a href="#A1.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ A.3 Limitations ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> in the Appendix. Compared with the early-reflected target, replacing it with time-shifted anechoic clean targets yields substantial improvements on non-intrusive quality metrics (DNSMOS from 3.06 to 3.25, NISQA from 3.23 to 3.85, and UTMOS from 2.26 to 2.76) and ASR performance (CAcc from 87.62 to 89.41). The improvement in CAcc indicates that these quality gains do not come at the expense of hallucination.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As noted in Section <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Evaluation Metrics ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>, the intrusive and downstream metrics on the official leaderboard may not accurately reflect the performance of models trained with shifted anechoic speech targets, because the evaluation uses early-reflected speech as the reference. To correct for this, Table <a href="#A1.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ A.2 Ablation study ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> (Appendix) presents the same metrics computed using <span id="S3.SS5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">the original anechoic clean speech as the reference</span>. Under this consistent definition, shifted anechoic speech targets significantly outperform early-reflected ones. These findings indicate that using early-reflected speech as the learning target still degrades the output quality of USE models, leading to enhanced audio that remains noticeably <span id="S3.SS5.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">reverberant</span>. Spectrogram comparison in Figure <a href="#A1.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ A.3 Limitations ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> (Appendix) and audio examples on our demo page further illustrate this effect.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S3.T1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 1</span>: </span><span id="S3.T1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Non-blind test set results of the URGENT 2025 Challenge. All metrics are “higher is better”, except MCD and LSD. Rank <math id="S3.T1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the system ranked <math id="S3.T1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N^{th}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N^{th}</annotation></semantics></math> in the challenge. Note that shaded metrics are not directly comparable across the two learning targets due to mismatches in the definition of the “clean” reference. See Tables <a href="#A1.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ A.2 Ablation study ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> to  <a href="#A1.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ A.2 Ablation study ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> in the Appendix for the ablation studies using the original anechoic clean speech as the reference.</span></figcaption>

</section>
<section id="S3.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.6 </span>Results of the Two-Stage Combination of Regression and Generative Models</h3>

<div id="S3.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To verify that the two-stage framework enables the GAN to focus primarily on correcting over-smoothed regions while leaving well-predicted region intact, we compute the average correlation coefficient between two magnitude-residual spectrograms on the non-blind test set: the ‘clean–regression residual’ (clean speech <math id="S3.SS6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> minus regression output <math id="S3.SS6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{s}</annotation></semantics></math>) and the ‘final–regression residual’ (final output <math id="S3.SS6.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{s}</annotation></semantics></math> minus regression output <math id="S3.SS6.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{s}</annotation></semantics></math>). We obtain a high correlation of 0.78, indicating that the GAN corrections are strongly aligned with the residual errors of the regression model and thus largely preserve signal fidelity (see Figures <a href="#A1.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ A.3 Limitations ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> and <a href="#A1.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ A.3 Limitations ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> in Appendix for spectrogram visualization).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">From Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3.5 Results of Applying Time-Shifted Anechoic Clean Speech as Learning Targets ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, we observe that applying GAN refinement to the regression output consistently and significantly improves NISQA, SpkSim, and CAcc, with moderate gains in UTMOS, while having only marginal or negligible impact on most intrusive SE metrics. This suggests that fidelity is well preserved while perceptual quality and downstream performance are enhanced. The overall ranking of the non-blind test set is summarized in Table <a href="#A1.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ A.3 Limitations ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> in the Appendix, where <span id="S3.SS6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GAN correction leads to an improved leaderboard rank</span>. To further compare our two-stage framework with other GAN training paradigm, Figure <a href="#A1.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ A.3 Limitations ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> (Appendix) plots the validation learning curves for a convention approach (pre-training with a regression loss followed by adversarial fine-tuning) versus our two-stage GAN correction. Across training, our two-stage framework consistently achieves lower magnitude, phase, and time-domain losses, as well as higher PESQ scores.
<span id="S3.SS6.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">In summary, the shifted anechoic target combined with GAN correction attains state-of-the-art performance across all non-intrusive metrics and ASR CAcc on the URGENT 2025 non-blind test set.</span> Ablation studies evaluating the effects of the three proposed techniques, with the original anechoic clean speech as the reference, are reported in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS2" title="A.2 Ablation study ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS7" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.7 </span>Subjective Evaluation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To subjectively evaluate audio quality under different USE settings, we conducted a listening test using a 5-point scale. A total of 23 participants listened to the audio samples and rated them from 1 (poor quality) to 5 (excellent quality).
Ten English utterances were randomly selected for each condition: noisy input, USE using early reflected target, shifted anechoic target, and shifted anechoic target + GAN. The average quality scores for these conditions are 1.86, 3.00, 3.68, and 3.97, respectively, with 95% confidence intervals of 0.19, 0.26, 0.20, and 0.19. These results verify the effectiveness of the proposed method and are consistent with the trends observed in the corresponding objective metrics. Some audio samples are available at <a href="https://jasonswfu.github.io/USE/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://jasonswfu.github.io/USE/</a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
