</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We next compare our proposed USE model (shifted anechoic target + GAN correction) with other popular open-source USE models, ClearerVoice-Studio <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2025</a>)</cite><span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
              
              
              
            https://github.com/modelscope/ClearerVoice-Studio</span></span></span>
and Resemble Enhance<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
              
              
              
            https://github.com/resemble-ai/resemble-enhance</span></span></span>
. Although this comparison is not strictly controlled due to differing training data, it still offers useful insight into the relative strengths and limitations of existing approaches. Since ClearerVoice-Studio supports only 16 kHz and 48 kHz inputs, and Resemble Enhance only 44.1 kHz, we evaluate on the corresponding subsets of the URGENT 2025 non-blind test set, as reported in Table <a href="#S3.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 3.8 Comparison with Other Open-Source USE Models ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.
Our proposed method outperforms ClearerVoice-Studio, a regression-based model built on MossFormer2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, although ClearerVoice-Studio still achieves reasonable enhancement quality. Resemble Enhance, based on latent conditional flow matching, substantially improves non-intrusive quality metrics but yields low intrusive scores and CAcc, suggesting a tendency to hallucinate content, which is consistent with prior findings on purely generative models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Saijo et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>

</figure>
<div id="S3.SS9.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS9.p1.1" class="ltx_p">One emerging application of USE is training data cleaning for downstream speech generative models (e.g., text-to-speech) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koizumi et al., 2023c</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Karita et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koizumi et al., 2023b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. This is particularly important for low-resource languages, where studio-quality recordings are scarce. To support this use case, the USE model must be <span id="S3.SS9.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">language-agnostic</span>. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Saijo et al. (2025)</a></cite> report that regression models are relatively insensitive to language variations, whereas purely generative models (e.g., latent diffusion and neural vocoders) tend to be more language dependent. This observation also motivates our two-stage design, where the generative model is used only to refine over-smoothed regions of a regression model’s output.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS9.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS9.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Following Miipher-2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Karita et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, we use the FLEURS dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Conneau et al., 2023</a>)</cite> to evaluate model performance on unseen languages. We select three languages (Italian, Dutch, and Japanese) and assess speech quality with DNSMOS, speaker similarity (relative to the original) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Desplanques et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, and ASR CAcc <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al., 2023</a>)</cite> before and after different speech restoration, as summarized in Table <a href="#S3.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 3.9 Evaluation on Unseen Languages ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. We also include FLEURS-R <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, a restored version of FLEURS processed by Miipher-2, obtained from the official release<span id="footnote4" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">4</span>
              
              
              
            https://huggingface.co/datasets/google/fleurs-r</span></span></span>. Miipher-2 uses acoustic features extracted by the Universal Speech Model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2023b</a>)</cite>, pre-trained on 12 million hours of speech across more than 300 languages, and reconstructs back with the WaveFit vocoder <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koizumi et al., 2023a</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS9.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS9.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We observe that some FLEURS samples contain only mild stationary wideband noise or electrical microphone hiss (see Figure <a href="#A1.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ A.3 Limitations ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> in the Appendix), artifacts that still appear in our training data even after VQScore filtering. Our original model (shifted anechoic target + GAN) does not fully remove such low-level background noise, likely because some “clean” training examples remain imperfect and the model learns to preserve these subtle distortions. To address this, we fine-tune the model solely on the highest-quality subset of our training data (EARS), and denote the result as Proposed (EARS) in Table <a href="#S3.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 3.9 Evaluation on Unseen Languages ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. Although FLEURS-R achieves slightly higher DNSMOS, its speaker characteristics deviate more from the original speech compared to our proposed methods, highlighting the fidelity-quality trade-off. Namely, some generative restoration may enhance perceptual quality at the expense of speaker similarity. Between our two proposed variants, Proposed (EARS) provides better speech quality and ASR accuracy, reinforcing the importance of training data quality for USE.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS10" class="ltx_subsection">

<td id="S3.T4.5.1.5.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;"><span id="S3.T4.5.1.5.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">0.1373</span><span id="S3.T4.5.1.5.7.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> </span><math id="S3.T4.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo mathsize="0.900em">±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.T4.5.1.5.7.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> 0.0021</span></td></tr>
</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS10.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS10.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The scarcity of studio-quality data hinders progress in TTS modeling, particularly for low-resource languages. We investigate the hypothesis that TTS training data restored by our USE can alleviate these bottlenecks. We exclude high-resource English and experiment with a training dataset comprised of four European languages: French (7.3k hours), German (5.5k hours), Dutch (760 hours), and Italian (123 hours), sourced from CML-TTS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">Oliveira et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and Emilia-YODAS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, with a sampling rate of 22.05 kHz.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS10.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS10.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We employ Zero-Shot Koel-TTS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hussain et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, a state-of-the-art encoder-decoder Transformer TTS backbone. This model features an autoregressive decoder that generates speech tokens conditioned on a text transcript and a speaker audio prompt. The model contains approximately 378M parameters and operates on low-frame-rate (21.5 FPS) audio codec tokens encoded by NanoCodec <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">Casanova et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Text transcripts are processed using a ByT5 byte-level tokenizer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xue et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS10.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS10.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We train the multilingual TTS model following the configurations of Koel-TTS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hussain et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. We then evaluate the model on Dutch and Italian (unseen language during our USE training) using character error rate (CER), word error rate (WER), speaker similarity between context and generated audio, and Fréchet codec distance<span id="footnote5" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">5</span>
              
              
              
            Fréchet codec distance (FCD) adapts FID <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">Heusel et al., 2017</a>)</cite> to measure the distance between real and generated distributions in the codec’s dequantized embedding space.</span></span></span> (FCD). Table <a href="#S3.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 3.10 Application to TTS Training Data Cleaning ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> demonstrates substantial improvements across all metrics when both context and training target audio are enhanced by our USE model. Furthermore, we observe that the TTS model consistently benefits when either the context or target audio is enhanced, as detailed in Table <a href="#A1.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ A.3 Limitations ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> (Appendix). These experiments indicate that our USE model effectively unlocks the potential of existing large-scale, multilingual, noisy speech datasets for training high-quality TTS models.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This paper systematically investigates three critical challenges in developing USE models.
First, we show that time-shifted anechoic clean speech is a better dereverberation target than conventional early-reflected speech, improving both perceptual quality and downstream ASR performance. Second, motivated by the distortion–perception trade-off theory, we propose a simple two-stage framework that balances fidelity and perceptual quality by combining a regression model with a residual generative refinement model, correcting over-smoothed regions without hallucinations. Third, we demonstrate that USE performance is strongly limited by training data quality: rigorous filtering and fine-tuning on the cleanest subset consistently yields better enhancement. Finally, our model generalizes well across languages while preserving high fidelity, making it effective for improving training data for downstream speech generation tasks.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Appendix</h2>

<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>The Distortion-Perception Tradeoff</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The performance of a speech enhancement model can be characterized by two criteria: 1) fidelity, measured by the average proximity of estimated speech <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{s}</annotation></semantics></math> to the clean speech <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>, and 2) perceptual quality, the degree to which the distribution of <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{s}</annotation></semantics></math>
is close to that of <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>. To alleviate the hallucination problem in generative models, our goal is to <span id="A1.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">achieve minimal distortion under a given level of perceptual quality <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math></span>. Mathematically, we are dealing with
the distortion-perception (DP) function  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>,</p>
<table id="A1.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D(P)=\min_{p_{\tilde{s}\mid y}}\{\;\mathbb{E}\!\left[d(s,\tilde{s})\right]\quad\text{s.t.}\quad d_{p}\!\left(p_{s},p_{\tilde{s}}\right)\leq P\}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><munder><mi>min</mi><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></msub></munder><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.280em" stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mpadded style="width:0.497em;" width="0.497em"><mi>𝔼</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mtext>s.t.</mtext></mrow><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D(P)=\min_{p_{\tilde{s}\mid y}}\{\;\mathbb{E}\!\left[d(s,\tilde{s})\right]\quad\text{s.t.}\quad d_{p}\!\left(p_{s},p_{\tilde{s}}\right)\leq P\},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Here, <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="d(.,.)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mo>,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d(.,.)</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the distortion criterion and <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="d_{p}(.,.)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mo>,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{p}(.,.)</annotation></semantics></math> denotes a divergence measure between two probability distributions. As shown in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>, <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D(P)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D(P)</annotation></semantics></math> is <span id="A1.SS1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">monotonically non-increasing and convex</span> under most commonly used divergence measures. Thus, traversing this function (or near this region) reveals a <span id="A1.SS1.p1.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">trade-off between distortion and perceptual quality</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Following  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>, we consider squared-error distortion <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d(s,\tilde{s})=\lVert s-\tilde{s}\rVert_{2}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.1389em">=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>−</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d(s,\tilde{s})=\lVert s-\tilde{s}\rVert_{2}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> and the Wasserstein
distance <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{p}\!\left(p_{s},p_{\tilde{s}}\right)=W_{2}\!\left(p_{s},p_{\tilde{s}}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{p}\!\left(p_{s},p_{\tilde{s}}\right)=W_{2}\!\left(p_{s},p_{\tilde{s}}\right)</annotation></semantics></math>.
Then, Equation (<a href="#A1.E4" title="In A.1 The Distortion-Perception Tradeoff ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>) can be written as:</p>
<table id="A1.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D(P)=\min_{p_{\tilde{s}\mid y}}\{\;\mathbb{E}\!\left[\lVert s-\tilde{s}\rVert_{2}^{2}\right]\quad\text{s.t.}\quad W_{2}\!\left(p_{s},p_{\tilde{s}}\right)\leq P\}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><munder><mi>min</mi><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></msub></munder><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.280em" stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mpadded style="width:0.497em;" width="0.497em"><mi>𝔼</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>−</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mtext>s.t.</mtext></mrow><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D(P)=\min_{p_{\tilde{s}\mid y}}\{\;\mathbb{E}\!\left[\lVert s-\tilde{s}\rVert_{2}^{2}\right]\quad\text{s.t.}\quad W_{2}\!\left(p_{s},p_{\tilde{s}}\right)\leq P\},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Note that, without any constraints, the minimal distortion <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>D</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> can be easily achieved by <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s^{*}=\mathbb{E}[s\mid y]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s^{*}=\mathbb{E}[s\mid y]</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">If <math id="A1.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{s}</annotation></semantics></math> is independent of <math id="A1.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> given <math id="A1.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>, the first term in Equation (<a href="#A1.E5" title="In A.1 The Distortion-Perception Tradeoff ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>) can be written as <math id="A1.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}\!\left[\lVert s-\tilde{s}\rVert^{2}\right]=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\lVert s-s^{*}\rVert^{2}\right]+\mathbb{E}\!\left[\lVert s^{*}-\tilde{s}\rVert^{2}\right]=D^{*}+\mathbb{E}\!\left[\lVert s^{*}-\tilde{s}\rVert^{2}\right]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mpadded style="width:0.497em;" width="0.497em"><mi>𝔼</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><msup><mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>−</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mpadded style="width:0.497em;" width="0.497em"><mi>𝔼</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><msup><mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:0.497em;" width="0.497em"><mi>𝔼</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><msup><mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>−</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>D</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>+</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:0.497em;" width="0.497em"><mi>𝔼</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><msup><mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>−</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}\!\left[\lVert s-\tilde{s}\rVert^{2}\right]=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\lVert s-s^{*}\rVert^{2}\right]+\mathbb{E}\!\left[\lVert s^{*}-\tilde{s}\rVert^{2}\right]=D^{*}+\mathbb{E}\!\left[\lVert s^{*}-\tilde{s}\rVert^{2}\right]</annotation></semantics></math>. The DP function can therefore be rewritten as:</p>
<table id="A1.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D(P)=D^{*}+\min_{p_{\tilde{s}\mid y}}\{\;\mathbb{E}\!\left[\lVert s^{*}-\tilde{s}\rVert_{2}^{2}\right]\quad\text{s.t.}\quad W_{2}\!\left(p_{s},p_{\tilde{s}}\right)\leq P\}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>D</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>+</mo><mrow><munder><mi>min</mi><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></msub></munder><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.280em" stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mpadded style="width:0.497em;" width="0.497em"><mi>𝔼</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>−</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mtext>s.t.</mtext></mrow><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D(P)=D^{*}+\min_{p_{\tilde{s}\mid y}}\{\;\mathbb{E}\!\left[\lVert s^{*}-\tilde{s}\rVert_{2}^{2}\right]\quad\text{s.t.}\quad W_{2}\!\left(p_{s},p_{\tilde{s}}\right)\leq P\},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">The minimal distortion under perfect perceptual quality, denoted by <math id="A1.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D(0)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D(0)</annotation></semantics></math> (i.e., <math id="A1.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math>=0, which implies <math id="A1.SS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{2}\!\left(p_{s},p_{\tilde{s}}\right)=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{2}\!\left(p_{s},p_{\tilde{s}}\right)=0</annotation></semantics></math>, and hence the constraint become <math id="A1.SS1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\tilde{s}}=p_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\tilde{s}}=p_{s}</annotation></semantics></math>), is given by:</p>
<table id="A1.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>

</table>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Since the objective (<math id="A1.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}\!\left[\lVert s^{*}-\tilde{s}\rVert_{2}^{2}\right]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mpadded style="width:0.497em;" width="0.497em"><mi>𝔼</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>−</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}\!\left[\lVert s^{*}-\tilde{s}\rVert_{2}^{2}\right]</annotation></semantics></math>) depends only on <math id="A1.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{s^{*}\tilde{s}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{s^{*}\tilde{s}}</annotation></semantics></math>, we can rewrite the constraint as:</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<table id="A1.E8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(8)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A1.SS1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Pi(p_{s},p_{s^{*}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Pi(p_{s},p_{s^{*}})</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the set of all joint distributions with marginals <math id="A1.SS1.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{s}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A1.SS1.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{s^{\ast}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{s^{\ast}}</annotation></semantics></math>. Because the second term in Equation <a href="#A1.E8" title="In A.1 The Distortion-Perception Tradeoff ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> corresponds to the Wasserstein distance between <math id="A1.SS1.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{s}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A1.SS1.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{s^{*}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{s^{*}}</annotation></semantics></math>, we finally obtain:</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<table id="A1.E9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D(0)=D^{*}+W_{2}\!\left(p_{s^{*}},p_{s}\right)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>D</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D(0)=D^{*}+W_{2}\!\left(p_{s^{*}},p_{s}\right),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(9)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Therefore, we can minimize the MSE while satisfying the perfect-perception constraint by <span id="A1.SS1.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">optimally transporting</span> the posterior mean prediction (<math id="A1.SS1.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{s^{\ast}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{s^{\ast}}</annotation></semantics></math>) to the real data distribution (<math id="A1.SS1.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{s}</annotation></semantics></math>). Following this formulation, as illustrated in Figure <a href="#S2.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 2.2 Bridging Fidelity and Quality: A Two-Stage Framework ‣ 2 Proposed Method ‣ Rethinking Training Targets, Architectures and Data Quality for Universal Speech Enhancement" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, our two-stage training first uses a frozen regression model to estimate the posterior mean, and then employs the GAN generator to optimally transport this estimate toward the real data distribution by minimizing the Wasserstein distance. For a more detailed discussion of the properties of the DP function, please refer to  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite> and  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>

<td id="A1.T7.5.1.4.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t"><math id="A1.T7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3.20\times 10^{-68}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3.20</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>68</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.20\times 10^{-68}</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<td id="A1.T7.5.1.4.9" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t"><math id="A1.T7.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2.40\times 10^{-23}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2.40</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>23</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.40\times 10^{-23}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td id="A1.T7.5.1.4.10" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t">0.03</td></tr>
</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3 </span>Limitations</h3>

<div id="A1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conducted several internal tests of this model, including on real noisy speech recorded with our laptops and cellphones, and it generally performs reasonably well. However, we do observe some failure cases. For example, in packet loss concealment, when the loss duration is too long, the reconstructed phonemes are often incorrect. Without additional conditioning (e.g., phoneme-based speech infilling or audio-visual speech enhancement using visual cues), and especially in multilingual settings, long-duration packet loss concealment remains a challenging task. Furthermore, due to its non-causal design, the model is not suitable for real-time applications; extending the framework to a causal setting is an important direction for future work.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<figure id="A1.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2603.02641v4/figs/RIR.png" id="A1.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:286/191;" width="286" height="191" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A1.F4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="A1.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">An example of a room impulse response, highlighting the time shift
